April 29th, 2026 / 11:00AM GMT, TotalEnergies 1Q2026 Earnings Call 
 
CORPORATE PARTICIPANTS 
Patrick Pouyanné - TotalEnergies SE - Chairman & CEO 
Jean-Pierre Sbraire - TotalEnergies SE - CFO 
 
Q&A PARTICIPANTS 
Michele Della Vigna - Goldman Sachs 
Biraj Borkhataria - RBC  
Lydia Rainforth - Barclays 
Martijn Rats - Morgan Stanley 
Douglas Leggate - Wolfe Research 
Lucas Herrmann – BNP Paribas Exane 
Alastair Syme – Citi 
Mark Wilson – Jefferies Equity Research 
Kim Fustier - HSBC 
Matt Lofting - JPMorgan 
Christopher Kuplent - Bank of America 
Henri Patricot - UBS  
Fergus Neve - Rothschild & Co. Redburn 
Jean-Luc Romain – CIC-CIB 
Anish Kapadia – Palissy Advisors  
Bertrand Hodée – Kepler Chevreux  
 
April 29th, 2026 / 11:00AM GMT, TotalEnergies 1Q2026 Earnings Call 
 
PRESENTATION 
Patrick Pouyanné - TotalEnergies SE - Chairman & CEO 
Good afternoon or good morning, everyone. Happy to be with you again today. So, before Jean-Pierre goes through 
the details of this first quarter financials, I would like first to make a few opening remarks in particular on the conflict 
in the Middle East and its consequences.  
As you know, this region, Middle East, holds, of course, a very special place for TotalEnergies. It's deeply rooted in our 
DNA, in our history, in our identity, because it is where the Company was born in 1924, in Iraq. And more importantly, 
this is a region where we have established, along the years, a prime position which differentiates us.  
Since the very first day of the conflict on February 28, our priority has been first the security of our teams and their 
families. We have decided, just two days after, to organize the evacuation of employees’ families and as well as some 
non-essential employees out of the UAE, Qatar, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Lebanon. Thanks to the strong 
mobilization in all our affiliates in the regions, but also around the globe and also at the headquarters, more than 1,300 
people have returned safely from the countries concerned by the conflict, and I want to thank all the teams who 
participated to that strong effort.  
Safety of our staff will remain our utmost priority, but I want also to reiterate here our full solidarity and support for 
the population of these countries which suffers as a consequence of the conflicts. I want to reaffirm TotalEnergies' 
commitment to all our local partners, contractors, and customers.  
From this point of view, I want to underline that we kept a presence in all the countries, along our partners. For example, 
in Abu Dhabi, all our secondees working for the ADNOC JVs are maintained on the ground. It's the same situation in 
Qatar. We have also sent some experts to assist QatarEnergy in evaluating the damage and the repairs necessary to 
the two LNG trains which were damaged during the conflict.  
We have maintained a team in Iraq, in Basra, of 20 TotalEnergies’ staff, who are supervising the progress of the GGIP 
projects on the ground, with around 5,000 workers there. And also in Saudi Arabia, we have, of course, maintained 
most of our secondees in order to supervise the Amiral project, which mobilizes today 22,000 workers.  
So, my message on this, first, is to thank all our teams which are again working hard in the region facing the situation. 
I went myself last week to visit them, and I can tell you I had a strong feeling of high mobilization of everybody facing 
these adverse events. And also, I met, of course, our partners and authorities to reaffirm our commitment to the region.  
Of course, we will have to draw some lessons from what happened, in particular to envisage some alternative 
evacuation routes for the production of oil in the region, but that will come after the conflict. This conflict immediately 
has some impact on TotalEnergies' operations. And we have been, by the way, very transparent, since day one, to 
disclose all the impacts on our activities.  
At this stage, production is shut down in Qatar, Iraq and UAE offshore, which represents approximately 15% of the total 
Oil & Gas production of the Company, more precisely, 360,000 barrels per day, because we continue to produce 
onshore UAE production, oil productions of 210,000 barrels per day TotalEnergies’ share, which is evacuated through 
Fujairah terminal, out of the Strait of Hormuz. And we also continue to produce Dolphin gas between Qatar and UAE 
because it's a domestic Gulf production.  
April 29th, 2026 / 11:00AM GMT, TotalEnergies 1Q2026 Earnings Call 
 
While this is a significant portion of our Upstream production, these Middle Eastern assets contribute less to our cash 
flow per barrel than the rest of our portfolio due to higher taxation in the region. This 15% of volumes, a little less, 
360,000 barrels per day, only account for roughly 10% of our Upstream cash flow at 60 $/b.  
The Company's cash-accretive growth expected for 2026 is largely outside the Middle East, and you've seen that 
through the results of the first quarter. Meaning that the higher oil price observed since the start of the crisis, more 
than offsets, of course, the loss of production in the Middle East. An equivalent of 8 $/b increase in the Brent is enough 
to offset the expected 2026 cash flow from the shut-in production. And we are, of course, today, more 100 $/b, I think 
even 115 $/b this morning, which in terms of our sensitivity to price, represents substantial additional cash flows.  
The impact of the LNG production shutdowns in Qatar or in Abu Dhabi on our LNG trading activities are, in fact, very 
limited, as our exposure to our marketing portfolio is limited to 1.5 Mt for the remainder of 2026. I remind you that 
most of the LNG produced by our JVs in Qatar are, in fact, marketed by QatarEnergy itself and not by TotalEnergies.  
Finally, on our refining activities in the region, the SATORP site, which is owned jointly by Aramco and TotalEnergies, 
was impacted by strikes that occurred during the night of April 7 to April 8, causing damage to three units. No casualties 
were reported. As a safety precaution, the units were immediately shut down. A partial restart occurred on April 14, 
allowing production to resume at a 50% capacity, 230,000 barrels per day. And the repair work on one of the units, the 
VDU, is well underway, and we expect to restart and to increase production to more than 300,000 barrels per day from 
the early days of May, May 5 or around. So that's the situation for assets.  
But this conflict, of course, has consequences beyond the only perimeter of TotalEnergies, and now will impact the 
course of 2026 very significantly in terms of markets. Of course, the damage to Upstream assets has been limited so 
far. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz constitutes a major disruption to the world energy system, as it affects around 
20% of worldwide crude oil, refined products and, of course, LNG exports. And there is very limited spare capacity of 
production outside the Gulf, in reality.  
The immediate consequence was a surge in oil prices, which are now around 100 to 115 $/b, which have been extremely 
volatile, with major swings in the past weeks. Some days have been the highest days, I even think we experienced eight 
of the ten highest volatile days in the last 25 years during the months of March and April.  
So given the time required to restart facilities, but also more importantly, to reach the final markets because an oil 
tanker which will be loaded in Abu Dhabi or in Saudi Arabia will take 25 days of shipping to reach its customers in Asia, 
Korea, Japan, and so there is a time lag. Even if the war was to end quickly, prices are expected to remain at high levels. 
And in all the scenarios I can read, and I agree with the scenarios I'm reading, either from the IMF or from some banks, 
at least 80 $/b is expected for 2026.  
In fact, the reality is that the 2026 surplus scenario that was anticipated by the markets and by us, by the way, at the 
beginning of the year, is now over, is behind us, with global hydrocarbon inventories being materially drawn to balance 
the market, already at a pace of 10 to 13 million barrels of oil per day. We have already consumed, I would say, 500 
million barrels out of inventories. And with the phenomenon I described, to restart and to reach the market, it's 
probably more in the range of 1 billion barrels, which will at least be consumed from the inventories. We would exit 
even if the conflict, and I hope so, will end in the month of May, we would exit the conflict with clearly some very low 
inventories.  
This conflict also has some impacts on the LNG markets and prices. We have seen that the European gas price 
established today at around 15 $/MBtu. But, again, we are facing now, by this summertime, the peak season for LNG 
because it's not only the warm summer season in Asia which will call for more LNG demand but also, it will be the 
April 29th, 2026 / 11:00AM GMT, TotalEnergies 1Q2026 Earnings Call 
 
season where Europe will have to replenish its storage. And as you know, at the end of the winter season, we were at 
the lowest point of the last five years in terms of European gas storage, around 25%. And we anticipate as well, and I 
was in Qatar, that QatarEnergy will wait for real stabilization of the Strait of Hormuz before they restart the liquefaction 
plants. You cannot turn on and turn off these plants easily. It will also impact the time it will take to reach the market. 
So that's on LNG. And I would not be surprised to see some support for higher prices by summer season, considering 
this timeline or time lag that LNG could go back to the market, and Qatar’s LNG represent almost 20% of the world 
market.  
So, in this context, strategy of TotalEnergies demonstrates once again the ability of the Company to capture price 
upsides, thanks to major strategic strengths of the Company. And also, I must say and I compliment the teams because 
of the strong operational performance, which of course is of essence in such markets during the first quarter. First, of 
course, we are integrated along the value chains of oil, gas, LNG, and electricity. It allows us to capture margins and 
prices all along the value chains and provides us with a unique combination of activities in oil, gas, and electricity: being 
a low-cost producer, transforming them into added value products which can then be traded on the market and sold 
to our B2B, B2C customers.  
Secondly, we are a growing Company, with strong organic growth. Then we are demonstrating, quarter after quarter, 
our ability to strongly grow our production, as you have seen a 4% year-over-year organic production growth for the 
Oil & Gas business and also, of course, our electricity business. 4% for Oil & Gas was above our annual guidance of 3%, 
which, of course, helps to offset, it was completely offset during the first quarter, and it will be partially during the 
second quarter, the impact of the Middle East conflict. But more importantly, it allows us to capture the upside of the 
high prices because the incremental production, the new production that we put on stream, is more accretive and 
generates more cash flow per barrel than the average of our portfolio.  
Third, we are diversified, and I think this is again a strong lesson in this crisis. Strong diversification and a rich and 
diversified portfolio allowed us to compensate again the impact of the crisis in the Middle East, from our geographically 
diversified portfolio of oil and LNG outside of the region. It notably allowed us to activate the flexibility of our LNG 
portfolio to ensure the security of supply of all our customers. And the diversity of the LNG portfolio - we are producing 
in eleven different countries - allowed us to serve our customers in Asia, re-rerouting some non-contracted volumes 
that we have in our portfolio to them, and not to declare any Force Majeure in our contracts. I can assure you, because 
I visited some customers in Asia, that they appreciated very much the value of the contract commitment at 
TotalEnergies.  
It's another example of the optionality of our diversified portfolio, and more than ever, the decision to restart the 
Mozambique LNG construction in January could be fully appreciated because it's a way of diversification which will be 
good for our portfolio by 2029. There was an article recently in a journal, saying that Mozambique will be the Qatar of 
Africa, and we are proud to build this project in Mozambique, and it will help us diversify. I would say as well, as we are 
working hard, these events are giving a good momentum to sanction Papua LNG before year-end.  
In this context, of course, compared to the beginning of the year where we were all cautious, there are no reasons not 
to fulfill all our commitments for strong returns to shareholders. And I think the Board has taken decisions yesterday 
that I'm happy to report to you. And considering, of course, the strength of the balance sheet, but also the environment 
and taking into account the ability to demonstrate our growth, priority was again given to what I call the sacrosanct 
dividend, by continuing our strong track record of dividend growth. We have decided to increase the first interim 
dividend by 5.9%, above probably market's expectation, to 0.9 €/share, compared to last year’s interim dividend, which 
April 29th, 2026 / 11:00AM GMT, TotalEnergies 1Q2026 Earnings Call 
 
was 0.85 €/share. We confirm once again the leadership of TotalEnergies, not only in terms of dividend resiliency, but 
also more important, dividend growth among the Oil & Gas majors.  
Secondly, we are, very pragmatic and consistent once again, in view of the current projections of the evolution of the 
prices, not only the second quarter, but as I said, along the year 2026, the Board of Directors gave us the authorization 
to continue, of course, the share buyback program up to the high end of the range that we gave last February, which 
was 750 M$ to 1.5 B$ per quarter. We'll target the high end of this range, up to 1.5 B$ per quarter.  
The Board also reiterates the objective to achieve a cash payout ratio above 40% for the full year 2026, and we will 
monitor buybacks accordingly throughout the year. Keep as well in mind that in terms of capital allocation, Board 
attached great importance to deleverage the balance sheet, and we would be happy to see it gearing in the low 10s by 
the end of 2026 if the crude oil price were to remain above 100 $/b.  
On that note, I will turn now the call to Jean-Pierre who will go through the details of the first quarter’s financials. 
Jean-Pierre Sbraire - TotalEnergies SE - CFO 
Thank you, Patrick. I will start by commenting on the price environment in the first quarter versus the fourth quarter 
of 2025. Brent averaged 81 $/b during the first quarter versus nearly 64 $/b in the fourth quarter of 2025, up more 
than 25%. And average liquid price was up by 12.4 $/b due to the time lag effect in particular in the United Arab 
Emirates.  
TTF averaged 13.7 $/MBtu versus 10.3 $/MBtu during the fourth quarter of 2025. And our average LNG price stayed at 
8.5 $/MBtu, oil price increase impacting LNG prices with one or two months of lag time according to LNG pricing 
formulas.  
Finally, the European refining margins remain at 11.4 $/b on average over the quarter, with exceptional margins in 
March and poor margins in January and February.  
In this price environment, the Company reported very strong financial results, with first quarter of 2026 cash flow of 
8.6 B$, increasing by 20% compared to the fourth quarter of 2025 and adjusted net income increasing by more than 
40% to 5.4 B$. These results, as already highlighted by Patrick, were possible because of strong operational 
performance of all businesses, which demonstrated the Company's ability to fully capture the environment upsides.  
Upstream delivered a 4% Upstream underlying accretive production growth, offsetting the production loss due to the 
crisis in the Middle East. In Downstream, the very good operational performance of our refineries, with the utilization 
rate on average over the quarter, above 90%, allowed us to capture high refining margins in March. And trading was 
also able to take benefits from the high market volatility in March and delivered high performance on crude, petroleum 
products, but also LNG.  
TotalEnergies has delivered a strong profitability this quarter, with return on equity at 14.4% and ROACE at 12.7%. 
Now moving to the business segments and starting with hydrocarbons. On a year-on-year basis, excluding the impact 
of the Middle East conflict, first quarter Oil & Gas production exceeded expectations and increased by more than 4%, 
above the guidance provided of 3% for 2026. As communicated by the Company from the very beginning, the 
production was impacted by the conflict in the Middle East, with an impact of around 100,000 barrels per day on 
average for the quarter, which correspond, on average, to around 25 days of disruption during the month of March. 
April 29th, 2026 / 11:00AM GMT, TotalEnergies 1Q2026 Earnings Call 
 
Turning to quarterly results and starting with E&P division, the segment generated an adjusted net operating income 
of 2.6 B$ this quarter, up by more than 40% quarter-to-quarter, fully capturing the increase in average liquids price of 
12.4 $/b over the quarter and demonstrating the accretiveness of the new projects. This quarter, Lapa SW in Brazil and 
Mabruk in Libya started up and will each, once ramped up, bring an additional production capacity of 25,000 barrels oil 
equivalent per day. Similarly, cash flow reached, for E&P, 4.6 B$, up 26% quarter-to-quarter. On the cost side, once 
again, we maintained our leadership, with an average Opex below 5 $/boe in the first quarter of 2026.  
On integrated LNG, on the production side, LNG production has grown significantly by 12% quarter-to-quarter, mainly 
supported by growth in Australia, with Ichthys LNG back to full capacity during the quarter, the United States and 
Malaysia. First quarter LNG sales reached 12.4 million tons, supported by strong spot activity, giving us a strong start 
compared to our yearly guidance of more than 44 million tons. Supported by this growth and strong trading activity 
capturing market volatility, the adjusted net operating income of Integrated LNG increased significantly quarter-to-
quarter to 1.3 B$ and cash flow to 1.8 B$. Given the evolution of the Oil & Gas prices in recent months and the lag 
effect on pricing formulas I already mentioned, the Company anticipates an average LNG selling price of around 
10 $/MBtu for the second quarter of 2026. As we execute our consistent strategy in LNG, the main milestone of the 
quarter was the full restart of construction activity at our Mozambique LNG project, with more than 6,000 people 
already on site as we speak. This project will broaden the diversification of our LNG supply, a strength that the current 
crisis has put additional emphasis on.  
Turning to Integrated Power now. Net power production increased year-on-year to 11.7 TWh, with a 20% growth of 
power generation from renewables, offsetting the lower utilization of gas flexible capacities in the context of lower 
winter demand in Europe and in the United States. TotalEnergies has increased its renewable capacity by nearly 8 GW 
over a 12-month period, on track to reach its objective of 42 GW gross installed capacity at the end of the year.  
Cash flow from operations was 0.6 B$, as no farm-downs were registered during the first quarter of 2026, unlike in the 
fourth quarter of 2025. This quarter, again, we provide more granularity in Integrated Power financial performance, 
with a split in cash flow between production assets on one side, renewable and gas-fired plants, and sales activities on 
the other side, B2B, B2C, and trading. The former contributed 35% of the cash flow and the latter for 65%, in line with 
the first quarter of 2025, due to the seasonal nature of the marketing business, with more consumption obviously 
during the winter. And given the closing of EPH deal that we announced this morning, TotalEnergies has now a 50% 
interest in a portfolio of flexible power generation assets in Europe, and Integrated Power should then benefit in 2026 
from 10 TWh net power production, in line with the 15 TWh guidance given for a full year, and more than 500 M$ 
contribution to available cash flow in relation with this EPH deal.  
Moving to Downstream, and during the first quarter, Refining & Chemicals was able to capture the exceptional margins 
in March, thanks again to the high availability of the refineries which recovered their full operational performance. It 
was particularly the case in Port Arthur in the U.S. and Donges in France. Utilization rate reached 92% in the absence 
of planned turnarounds, and trading activities were also very strong for crude and products, taking benefits of the 
market volatility. Overall, for Refining & Chemicals, adjusted net operating income was up by nearly 600 M$ quarter-
to-quarter to 1.6 B$, and cash flow reached 1.7 B$. In Marketing & Services, results remain consistently strong and 
reflect the seasonality of the business, with higher margin activities offsetting lower volumes, linked to the disposal of 
some assets in Brazil and in Sahel in Africa.  
Moving to corporate, at Company level, and starting with working capital. Working capital increased by 5.1 B$ during 
the first quarter, out of which 2.5 B$ is related to guided business seasonality, and 2.6 B$ that reflects the impact of 
higher hydrocarbons prices at the end of the quarter, notably on inventories.  
April 29th, 2026 / 11:00AM GMT, TotalEnergies 1Q2026 Earnings Call 
 
While the context remained quite volatile, we deployed our investment program with discipline, with net investments 
that amounted to 4.5 B$ in the first quarter, with a neutral balance between acquisitions and disposals in line with our 
quarterly budget. We therefore reiterate full year 2026 net investment guidance of 15 B$. 
As a result, the gearing lands at 15.5% at the end of the quarter, with cash flow growth driven by higher energy prices, 
partially offsetting in particular the impact of high prices on the working capital.  
Looking forward now, we expect to maintain strong momentum with hydrocarbon production, excluding Middle East 
impact, in the second quarter, expected to grow around 4% compared to the second quarter of 2025, in line with the 
growth we registered during the first quarter. As we speak, as mentioned by Patrick, production shut down in the 
Middle East still represents around 15% of the Company's total production. And we anticipate refining utilization in the 
range 80% to 85% in the second quarter of 2026, which accounts for a two-month scheduled maintenance at Donges 
and the impact of the capacity reduction of SATORP commented by Patrick.  
As I mentioned, the Company confirmed it expects its yearly net investment to be at 15 B$ for the full year, in line with 
annual guidance. Therefore, net investments should trend downwards in the second quarter. Meanwhile, the Company 
is evaluating options to accelerate short-cycle investment to capture current hydrocarbon price environment. 
To conclude, this set of growing earnings clearly demonstrate, in our view, the strength of our integrated model in oil, 
gas and power, which enabled us to seize price upside in the first quarter and put us in a strong position for the second 
quarter and the rest of the year. 
With that, I think with Patrick, we are now available to answer your questions. You can open up the line for questions, 
please. 
 
 
April 29th, 2026 / 11:00AM GMT, TotalEnergies 1Q2026 Earnings Call 
 
 
QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS 
Michele Della Vigna - Goldman Sachs 
I wanted to ask two questions on LNG. The first one is about whether with all of this crisis, you're starting to see a 
resurgence of demand for oil-linked long-term contracts and if that can unlock more LNG projects for you, like for 
instance, PNG.  
But longer term, I was also wondering if this crisis may actually be a bit more concerning and reduce some of the 
dependence on hydrocarbons from Asia, for instance, turn some of those countries more towards coal, solar and energy 
storage as an alternative. And if that could actually make perhaps what already looks like probably an oversupplied 
LNG market from 2028 last well into the next decade. Thank you.  
Patrick Pouyanné - TotalEnergies SE - Chairman & CEO 
I will take the second one first, Michele. It's quite clear, for our customers in Asia, a crisis in 2022, another one in 2026, 
reliability from an affordability point of view of the LNG will be questioned. And that's why, by the way, we think we 
have to promote to them the idea of long-term contracts, not only related to spot price. That's very clear. That’s what 
the European countries, because of the rules, are not benefiting from. I think the current crisis should influence them 
and put them more on this type of long-term contract. You are right.  
That way, the whole planet, not only in Asia, the governments will look again to, like we were in the ‘70s, domestic 
production first, domestic energy first, whatever it is, coming from coal when you have coal, or coming from biofuels. 
By the way, Malaysia, Indonesia are beginning to raise their biodiesel content, very logically. But coming to renewables, 
of course, as well, and from this position of Company, TotalEnergies could benefit from it because we are also investing 
in electricity. And electrification will be also a global answer, because you can produce electricity from various means 
and not only from hydrocarbons. So that will be the other big trend, that we will see, because security of supply, 
because again affordability of energy is of essence. 
It's not very good news, I agree, for the LNG markets. As you said, probably the result of this crisis as well is that we 
push back some of the famous wave, I think, because there will be some delays in some projects, because we don't 
know today how long the war will last. We have no idea. I have always said that in 2026, we'll remain at a good price. I 
think that for 2027, we can be optimistic. Then what you said, the oversupply in LNG market will come from 2028. But 
I would say that it's not bad for customers to have an oversupplied market. One of the observations I've done, when I 
observe what happens today with the crisis, it's quite remarkable: I know only two markets today where there will be 
no impact of the crisis on the energy price. One was the U.S. domestic gas price, the Henry Hub, that still remains lower, 
at 3 $/MBtu instead of 4 before, or 3.5. Why? Because there is an oversupply, there is overcapacity. The Permian gas 
is now connected through pipelines.  
And the other market I observe is the French electricity market. No impact at all because also of overcapacities of 
nuclear and renewables, by the way, both. So we produce too much. And that means it is a way to secure the 
affordability. 
April 29th, 2026 / 11:00AM GMT, TotalEnergies 1Q2026 Earnings Call 
 
From this perspective, because of what you said, and the fear which could be generated to an LNG customer, the fact 
that we'll enter at a certain point - when? probably more summer 2028 than before or winter 2028 - a lower cycle, will 
be good to convince them to come to us.  
I’ll make a link with your first question. Honestly, today, I think we were happy and lucky to have signed a lot of oil-
linked contracts because in this context, where there is sort of a bullish price overall, we have always quite been bullish, 
but I think this context, the crisis, will also impact the oil markets. Because there will be now something which was even 
completely hypothetical, in fact only on the risk cartography, which was the closing of the Strait of Hormuz, which 
became a real possibility to materialize. This threat has materialized.  
And you have, in the Gulf, more than 20%, 25%, 30% of the Oil & Gas resource. Clearly, this will have an impact on the 
way that the markets will take this threat into consideration, even if we go down to a stabilized situation for Strait of 
Hormuz, it will have an impact on the markers, on the Middle East markers.  
Today, I think we are happy to see that. We see appetite from Asian buyers for Papua LNG, not only because of the 
contract, but because of the geographical position. Of course, Papua LNG is perfectly located, not far from them, 
outside. So any diversity is good. On our side as well, because of this geography, we will see if we sign long-term 
contracts for Papua LNG, or if we keep some LNG for our own portfolio because we like this LNG as well for our own 
portfolio. But, again, no problem on this perspective to sign and we might be, I would say, in this context, a little tougher 
in the negotiation.  
What I've observed the last week, some Asian buyers come back to “Henry Hub +” because they just observed what 
happens and the stable and affordable gas marker is the Henry Hub. I think that there will be quite a lot of new 
popularity for the “Henry Hub +” if some LNG offtakers want to sell their LNG there. 
But definitely, this crisis has an impact on all these global LNG markets. Having said that, you've seen our results during 
the first quarter. When you have a strong, diversified portfolio, you can do good results when you have volatility, and I 
think we demonstrated that with our teams during the first quarter. I think we'll continue for the next quarter as well. 
Biraj Borkhataria - RBC 
Thanks for taking my question and thank you for the comprehensive overview of your operations. The first one, just on 
the comment in the release around accelerating short-cycle investments. Could you just unpack that a little bit more? 
What opportunities are you looking at? And secondly, what are you looking to see macro-wise or otherwise to put that 
capital to work?  
And then, secondly, just a follow-up on Papua New Guinea. Could you just talk about the steps from here to FID? Are 
the fiscal terms all now agreed and tendered and so on? Just any uncertainties there at FID. Thank you. 
Patrick Pouyanné - TotalEnergies SE - Chairman & CEO 
First question, I mean, you would have been surprised that we didn't mention that, so I was sure I would have a 
question. So it's quite natural as CEO of the Company that I've asked my E&P teams “is there anything to accelerate on 
the short cycle to benefit from the higher price deck?” Because again, on 2026, I'm quite confident, it's difficult in this 
world, but to see at least 80 $/b, I think I would put quite a lot of my own money on it for the rest of the year. 
By the way, it's an exercise which is moving on. I know there are a few countries like Angola, for example, where they 
have some ideas. So if we need to dedicate a few hundred million dollars to that, I would do it. Maybe I will tell you at 
April 29th, 2026 / 11:00AM GMT, TotalEnergies 1Q2026 Earnings Call 
 
the end of the day, it's not 15 B$, but 15 to 15.5 B$. But you will accept it if it's profitable on the short term. Honestly, 
I'm not sure it's so big because, in fact, when we built the budget, we did not arbitrate a lot of short-term cycles. 
In fact, we had a list of what we could cancel in case the price of oil was going down to 50 $/b. So we prepared in case 
of adverse market. But we have asked the questions, and I know that because I visited some countries, they have some 
few ideas. I can be flexible on keeping the discipline. But, again, if we can generate some good free cash flow on the 
short term, everybody will appreciate it. So it is not probably as big as I just mentioned. It is probably a few hundred 
million dollars that we could mobilize, subject to capacity to have the rigs, et cetera. So, we are working on it with some 
countries.  
On Papua LNG, I think you know it’s a big project, good many partners. We have at least four workflows in parallel. The 
Capex side, I would say, and the EPC are progressing very well. We have made some recommendations to our partners. 
We are waiting for approval from one of them, I hope we will get it soon, so that we can move forward with these 
tenders.  
In parallel to that, we have, I would say, the financing of the project, because there is project financing. Both are linked, 
by the way, because as you know, selection of the nationality of some contractors had an impact on the involvement 
of export credit agencies. There's a little sequence there: we need to have decided the contractors so that we can 
definitely confirm to the different credit export agencies. I think there is some appetite clearly from Asian credit export 
agencies, but also we discussed with the U.S. ones about it. And so, we are moving on the financing of it as well. So 
that’s the second workflow.  
The third workflow, as you said, is a discussion with the government. We have progressed, I would say. I could almost 
say finalized, but I didn't see the ink on the paper. Between the government and ourselves, there is an understanding
